messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark is a 55-year-old counselor who has spent two decades helping others navigate their worst moments, yet he finds himself unable to navigate his own. He lives alone in a quiet apartment complex, and for the past eight months, since the fire at the community center where he was leading a support group, his life has contracted into a narrow, watchful existence. He came to therapy not because he wanted to, but because his supervisor at the county mental health agency noticed he had begun canceling his evening groups and avoiding the break room where someone once microwaved popcorn too long.

The fire started during a routine Tuesday evening session. A client, a young man who had been struggling with rage after a workplace accident, had become agitated during a check-in. Mark had seen escalation before and was reaching for the de-escalation script when the client suddenly swept a stack of papers and a coffee mug off the table. The ceramic mug shattered against the wall, and in the same instant, a faulty space heater in the corner sparked. The smell of burning dust and plastic filled the room before the smoke alarm even sounded. Mark remembers the client’s face, the way the man’s anger collapsed into terror as the smoke thickened. He remembers the smell—acrid, chemical, alive—and he remembers thinking, *I have to get everyone out*. He did. No one was hurt. But in the weeks that followed, Mark began to realize that he had not left that room.

The smell is what haunts him most. It returns without warning—the sharp, burnt smell of smoke and plastic—and when it does, his body reacts before his mind can catch up. His heart pounds, his palms sweat, and he feels a rush of adrenaline that leaves him trembling and disoriented. He has come to believe that his body has turned against him, that it keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is standing in his own kitchen or walking through a grocery store. What frightens him most is that sometimes the emotion arrives with no image at all. He will be sitting at his desk, reviewing case notes, and suddenly he is flooded with the same terror he felt that night, but there is no picture in his mind, no memory of the smoke or the client’s face—just the raw, unbearable feeling. He has started to feel that the memory itself does not belong to him. When he tries to recall the fire, it feels like a story he was told about someone else, not something he lived through. And yet his body remembers what his mind cannot claim.

Mark has become vigilant in a way that exhausts him. He scans every room he enters for loose objects, for things that could be thrown, for anything that might spark or smolder. He is certain that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will happen again. He monitors his own thoughts constantly, checking himself for signs that he is losing control, because he is afraid that if he allows himself to think about the event, he will not be able to handle it. He has stopped seeing his friends. They call, they leave messages, but he cannot bring himself to respond. He tells himself he is just busy, but the truth is that he is afraid of what might come up if he has to talk about his life. He is afraid that if someone asks him how he is, he will crack open.

At work, he has become a ghost. He still sees his individual clients, but he has stopped running the evening support groups. He avoids the staff lounge, where the faint smell of burnt coffee triggers a cold sweat. He eats lunch in his car. His supervisor has asked if he is okay, and Mark has said yes, because he does not know how to say that he is terrified of his own mind. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when a client, in a moment of frustration, slammed a notebook on the desk. Mark flinched so violently that he knocked over his chair. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood there, gripping the sink, trying to breathe. He realized that he could not keep pretending that he was fine. He is afraid that if he starts talking about the fire, he will never stop, that the feelings will drown him. But he is also afraid that if he does not, he will lose the only thing he has left—his ability to do the work that has given his life meaning.
